analysis.one_liner: Gives hourly retail, food service, warehouse, hospitality, and cleaning workers two weeks' schedule notice, extra pay for late changes, and a right to request stable hours.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 17, 2025 with 54 cosponsors, all Democrats; referred to four House committees, where it has sat without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give hourly workers in retail, food service, cleaning, hotels, and warehouses the right to ask their employer for steadier hours without being punished for asking. Employers in those industries would have to post work schedules at least 14 days ahead, pay extra when they change a schedule on short notice or split a worker's day into two shifts, and pay extra (1.5x) for shifts starting less than 11 hours after the last one ended. Workers who are denied a schedule change for health, caregiving, school, or a second job would get a stated reason, and the Labor Department plus private lawsuits would enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers in the covered industries — retail sales, food preparation and serving, cleaning, hotel staff, and warehouse workers. Roughly two-thirds of hourly retail and food service workers get less than two weeks' notice of their schedules, a third get less than one week, more than one in five have worked on-call shifts, and more than one in three have worked 'clopening' shifts (close at night, open the next morning). These workers would get advance notice, extra pay when employers disrupt their schedules, the right to refuse work not on the posted schedule, and a guaranteed shot at a schedule change for health, caregiving, school, or a second job. Workers of color, who the bill's findings say are more likely to face cancelled, on-call, and clopening shifts, would benefit disproportionately.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly retail, food service, warehouse, hotel, and cleaning workers

how_it_helps.text: Employers must give covered workers their schedules at least 14 days ahead and pay $75 per day for each day a schedule is late [S2].
Employers must pay an extra hour of wages when they add hours or change a shift on short notice, and half-time pay for scheduled hours they cancel [S2].
Workers can decline, without penalty, any shift starting less than 11 hours after their previous shift ended ('clopening'), or work it at 1.5x pay with written consent [S2].

Any employee of a covered employer (15 or more workers) can request schedule changes for hours, times, location, notice, or steadiness; for requests tied to a serious health condition, caregiving, school or training, or a second job, the employer must grant the request or state a bona fide business reason for denying it [S2].

Retaliation for requesting changes or filing complaints is unlawful, with back pay, doubled liquidated damages, reinstatement, and attorney's fees available through the Labor Department or private lawsuits [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more workers, concentrated in retail, food service, hotels, cleaning contractors, and warehousing. They would bear the cost of advance scheduling, predictability and split-shift premiums, and the recordkeeping, posting, and compliance work the bill requires. Businesses would also lose the labor-cost flexibility of just-in-time scheduling, where workers absorb the uncertainty so labor hours can be matched hour-by-hour to customer traffic.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large retail, restaurant, hotel, cleaning, and warehouse employers

drawbacks.text: Scheduling premiums and the 14-day notice rule add real labor costs, and businesses argue that last-minute schedule changes driven by customer demand — weather, call-outs, surges — would become more expensive, which could push some employers toward fewer scheduled hours or more automation [S2].

The bill's enforcement creates litigation exposure: employers face liquidated damages (an amount equal to the underlying damages) that can be waived only if they prove a good-faith mistake, and private suits can proceed as collective actions on behalf of similarly situated employees [S2].

Even supporters describe this as 'a first step': the strongest protections (notice and pay rules) apply only to nonexempt workers in a few designated occupations, so salaried, exempt, and uncovered-industry workers get only the weaker right-to-request process [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for workers are concrete and the bill's own findings cite evidence that scheduling rules improved pay and stability in ten cities and Oregon, and that a controlled experiment at Gap stores raised sales and productivity alongside worker well-being [S2]. The costs fall on employers, mainly the large chains that dominate retail, food service, and warehousing, and are real but modest relative to the pay those employers already owe. The main design weakness is narrow coverage: the strongest rules reach only the designated low-wage occupations, leaving many hourly workers outside them. On balance this is a well-targeted bill whose costs land on a concentrated industry and whose benefits land on its lowest-paid workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was just introduced and referred to four House committees — Education and Workforce, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary — and no committee has taken it up yet [S4].

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro (D-CT) introduced the Schedules That Work Act on December 17, 2025 [S1][S4].
Fifty-four House members cosponsored the bill, every one of them a Democrat [S3].
The Speaker referred it to four committees at once, which means any single committee's inaction can keep the bill from moving; none has scheduled a hearing or markup [S4].
Earlier versions of the Schedules That Work Act in prior Congresses also died in committee without a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to act on the bill. Employers in retail, food service, hospitality, warehousing, and cleaning keep the current system — short notice, on-call and clopening shifts, cancelled hours at no cost to them — for as long as the bill sits unconsidered in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers keep the scheduling status quo

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Schedules That Work Act in the House on December 17, 2025.

for.name: 54 House Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including Representatives Adams, Casar, Jayapal, Ocasio-Cortez, Schakowsky, and Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction; no Republican cosponsored.

against.name: House Education and Workforce, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and have taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 54 cosponsors, plus lead sponsor Rosa DeLauro, are Democrats; no Republicans have signed on [S3].

industries.note: They would owe $75 per late-schedule day, an extra hour's pay for short-notice changes, half pay for cancelled scheduled hours, and split-shift premiums — costs that currently fall on workers as unpredictable hours. Their interest in keeping just-in-time scheduling runs directly against the stability workers would gain [S2].
Warehouse workers are covered sector employees, so scheduling rules would end demand-driven shift assignment in fulfillment operations [S2].
Hospitality establishments are expressly covered; hotel staff would get 14-day notice and premiums for late changes and clopening shifts [S2].
Cleaning occupations are covered sector employees subject to the notice and pay rules [S2].

The bill directs the Labor Department to run pilots using electronic workforce management systems to deliver flexible, predictable schedules, and employers would need better scheduling tools to comply — a modest commercial opportunity [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The 119th Congress is still in session, but the bill faces the usual path for a labor-standards bill from the House minority: sitting in committee without a hearing. Its referral to four committees makes movement harder, since any of them could claim jurisdiction and none is obligated to act. Similar Schedules That Work Act versions introduced in prior Congresses never reached a floor vote, and with no Republican cosponsors the bill is unlikely to advance in this House.
